'''''Amaranthus blitum''''', commonly called '''purple amaranth'''<ref name=PLANTS>{{PLANTS|id=AMBL2|taxon=Amaranthus blitum|accessdate=7 January 2016}}</ref> or '''Guernsey pigweed''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |accessdate=2014-10-17 }}</ref> is an annual plant species in the economically important plant family [[Amaranthaceae]]. It has a number of culinary uses.

==Description==
''Amaranthus blitum'' is an erect or semi-prostrate [[annual plant]]. The single or branched stem can grow to {{convert|1|m|ft|frac=2}} tall. The green or purplish [[leaves]] are up to {{convert|10|cm|4=0}} long on stalks of a similar length and are arranged spirally. They are simple, roughly triangular in shape and have entire margins.<ref name="Grubben" />

The [[inflorescence]] is a spike with the tiny male and female flowers clustered together. The fruits are small globular capsules containing disc-shaped seeds.<ref name="Grubben" />

=== Related plants ===
''[[Amaranthus viridis]]'', the slender amaranth or green amaranth, is closely related and edible.<ref>{{cite book |author=Grubben, G.J.H. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6jrlyOPfr24C&pg=PA88 |title=Vegetables |publisher=PROTA |year=2004 |isbn=978-90-5782-147-9 |page=88}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
Native to the Mediterranean region, it is naturalized in other parts of the world, including much of eastern North America,<ref name=PLANTS/> much of tropical Africa, Western Europe and Japan.<ref name=Grubben>{{cite book|author=Grubben, G.J.H.|title=Vegetables|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6jrlyOPfr24C&pg=PA63 |year=2004 |publisher=PROTA |isbn=978-90-5782-147-9 |pages=63–65}}</ref> In Britain it was first recorded in the wild in 1771 when it appeared in Essex. It occurred more frequently in scattered locations in southern England in the 19th century but has since decreased. It is established in Guernsey and elsewhere as a casual plant, springing up on waste ground, rubbish tips and cultivated areas, probably from wool waste, [[coir|coconut fibre]] or birdseed.<ref name=Grubben/>

==Uses==
Although not cultivated, this plant is gathered from the wild and eaten in many parts of the world.<ref name="prota">Grubben, G.J.H. & Denton, O.A. (2004) Plant Resources of Tropical Africa 2. Vegetables. PROTA Foundation, Wageningen; Backhuys, Leiden; CTA, Wageningen.</ref> The [[Greeks]] refer to ''A. blitum'' var. ''silvestre'' as {{lang|grc|vlita}} (Modern Greek: {{lang|el|βλίτα}}) and eat the leaves and the cooked tender shoots, served with [[olive oil]], [[lemon]] and [[salt]]. In [[Lebanon]] (especially to the north) a side dish is made from the young shoots; they are cooked in olive oil, onion, chilli, and [[burghul]], seasoned with salt and lemon, and eaten with [[pita]].<ref name=Grubben/>

==In culture==
The plant is thought by many to be the plant mentioned in the [[Mishnah]] (''Shevi'it'' 9:1), compiled in 189 [[Common Era|CE]], under the late Hebrew name ''yarbūzīn hashōtīn'' (wild amaranths).<ref>{{cite book |author-last=Amar |author-first=Z. |title=Flora and Fauna in Maimonides' Teachings |publisher= |year=2015 |location=Kfar Darom |pages=94 |language=he |oclc=783455868 |authorlink=Zohar Amar}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |title=The Mishnah |title-link=Mishnah |page=[https://archive.org/details/DanbyMishnah/page/49/mode/1up 49 (note 2)] |year=1933 |editor-last1=Danby |editor-first1=H. |contribution= |place=Oxford |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] |isbn=0-19-815402-X |editor-link1=Herbert Danby}}</ref>
